transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yeah, thanks. Um, what brings me in... well, it's—it's my talking, mostly. Or my thinking? I don't even know anymore, to be honest. I work as an orderly, you know, a psych aide over at the hospital, mostly doing the overnight shifts because the pay is a little better and I only have my high school diploma, so I have to take what I can get, right? 

But lately, I just... I can’t keep my words in a straight line anymore. It's like they're just spilling out all wrong. Like, the other morning, I was trying to give a quick rundown to the day-shift nurse about how my overnight shift went, just basic stuff about who slept and who didn't. But then suddenly I start talking about soccer, because I used to play back in school and someone had a ball on the TV, and then from there I'm talking about the paint colors on the walls in the dayroom, and then I'm jumping right back to the patient charts—but not even the right charts, just the concept of the folders themselves. 

And I can just see it in their faces. I can see everyone getting completely lost. The nurses look at me like I'm speaking a different language, and I'm standing there knowing I started at point A but somehow ended up at point Z, and I can't even retrace my steps to figure out how I got there. It's just happening all the time now. Every time I try to explain something simple, it turns into this huge tangled mess that doesn't connect, and it's making it really, really hard to do my job or even just have a normal conversation without people staring at me.
Do you use any recreational drugs or alcohol?

No, no, I don't. I mean, I know a lot of people my age do, especially working the night shift, you know? A lot of the guys I work with will go out for a drink at like 7 or 8 AM when our shift ends, which always seemed so weird to me, drinking in the morning while the sun is coming up and everyone else is just heading to work. But I guess it's their evening, right? So it makes sense for them. But no, I don't join them. I don't drink at all. 

And drugs, definitely not. Working as a psych aide, you see exactly what happens to people who come in on all sorts of stuff—meth, pills, even just really bad trips on weed or whatever they bought off the street. I see them in the unit all the time, pacing the halls, screaming at the walls, completely out of their minds, and I just... I never wanted to mess with my brain like that. I've always been really careful about it. And especially not right now, with how my head is already feeling so scrambled and my words are getting all tied up like I was just saying. I can't even imagine adding alcohol or drugs into this mess. It would just make everything a thousand times worse, wouldn't it? So, no, absolutely nothing like that. Not even a beer on the weekends. I just drink coffee, honestly. Lots and lots of coffee from the breakroom vending machine to stay awake for the overnight shifts, which probably tastes like dirt, but it keeps me upright. But yeah, definitely no drugs or alcohol.
Have you been hearing or seeing things that aren't there?

No, no, I haven't. Um, I know that's a thing that happens to a lot of the patients I work with, you know? They'll be staring at a blank wall having a full-blown argument with someone who isn't there, or swatting at things in the air that don't exist, but for me? No. I don't get any of that. 

I mean, don't get me wrong, working the overnight shift, your eyes can play tricks on you when you're staring down a long, dim hallway at three in the morning. Sometimes the fluorescent lights flicker in the C-wing—maintenance never fixes them because we're just the night shift, right, so we're always the bottom priority—and you might think you see a shadow move out of the corner of your eye. But if I turn and look, it's always just a linen cart, or a mop bucket someone left out, or maybe a patient who got up to pace around. I always know what it actually is. 

And hearing things... honestly, the ward is noisy enough as it is without my brain making things up. The ice machine down the hall makes this huge clunking sound every forty-five minutes that sounds exactly like someone dropping a heavy work boot on the linoleum, and the HVAC system has this constant, low hum that vibrates right through the soles of your shoes. So I hear all of that. But it's all real stuff, you know? I'm not hearing voices in my head or seeing visions or anything like that. I know exactly what's actually in the room with me. It's really just the talking thing I told you about, how my own words get all smashed together and I can't keep my sentences straight. But I'm definitely not seeing or hearing anything that isn't really there.
Do you feel like your thoughts are racing or speeding by really fast when this happens?

No, not really. It's not like that. It's not a speed thing, you know? Like, when I see the patients who are really manic, the ones who come in and they haven't slept in five days and they're pacing the dayroom at two in the morning, you can tell their brains are just going a million miles an hour. They talk so fast you can barely catch every third word, and they act like there's a motor inside them that just won't shut off. But that's not what's happening to me at all. 

My thoughts aren't racing. They're just... getting lost on the way out, I guess? Like, the speed is totally normal. If I'm thinking about the patient charts, I'm just thinking about them at a regular, boring, everyday pace. But then when I open my mouth to talk about the charts, the words just sort of... take a detour. It's like I'm driving the speed limit, completely normal, but someone swapped all the road signs on me, so I end up in a totally different town without even realizing I took a wrong turn. 

I'm not feeling rushed or pressured or anything. I don't feel like I have too many thoughts trying to squeeze through the door at the same time. It's just that the connections are broken. Like I said before, with the soccer and the paint colors and the folders. I wasn't rushing through that conversation. I was actually trying to be really careful and clear because I knew the day nurse, Brenda, was already annoyed that I was running a few minutes late with the handover. I was speaking at a totally normal pace. It just didn't make any sense. So, no, it's definitely not that my thoughts are racing or speeding by. It's just the words themselves that are all wrong.
Have you been feeling unusually sad, anxious, or irritable lately?

Yeah, sad. Definitely sad. I mean, not just sad like, "Oh, I had a bad day at work," but this deep, heavy kind of sad that just... it doesn't go away. It's like I wake up in the afternoon, because of the night shift, right? And before I even get out of bed, before my feet even hit the floor, I just feel this massive weight on my chest. It's just so heavy, and empty at the same time, if that even makes sense. Like there's nothing inside me but lead. 

And it's most days now. It really is. I'll drag myself out of bed, make that terrible coffee I told you about, put on my scrubs, and just sort of... go through the motions. But the whole time, I just feel so completely hollowed out. And then, when the shift is over, around 7 AM when everyone else is, you know, going to get their morning drinks or heading home to sleep... I get out to the parking lot, and the sun is coming up, and it's supposed to be a new day, but I just get into my car and I can't even put the key in the ignition. I just sit there behind the wheel, staring at the dashboard, and I just start crying. For no reason. I mean, nobody yelled at me, none of the patients threw anything at me that night, it was a totally normal shift, but I'll just sit in the driver's seat and cry for like twenty, thirty minutes before I can even pull myself together enough to drive the ten minutes back to my apartment. 

It's just this overwhelming sadness that I can't shake. I try to tell myself, you know, "You have a job, you're paying rent, you're doing fine," but my brain just doesn't care. It just feels like everything is pointless and exhausting. So yeah, definitely sad. Not really anxious or irritable, just... really, really sad and empty. All the time.
How long have you been experiencing these difficulties with your thoughts and words?

Well, the thing with my words getting all mixed up, that's been going on for a while now. It's not just a recent thing, you know? It's been... gosh, I'd say about a year and a month. Yeah, thirteen months. I remember exactly when it started because it was right around the time I first got this feeling that I was being watched. 

See, about a year and a month ago, I started noticing things at work. Little things at first. Like, I'd be walking down the C-wing, and I'd get this intense, prickling sensation on the back of my neck, like someone's eyes were just boring into me. I thought maybe it was one of the patients, you know, staring out from their room, but I'd turn around and the hallway would be completely empty. And then it started happening in the breakroom, too. I'd be sitting there, trying to eat my lukewarm microwave dinner at 2 AM, and I'd just know, with absolute certainty, that someone—or something—was observing me. Monitoring me. 

And it wasn't just at the hospital, either. I'd go home to my apartment, lock the door, pull the blinds down tight, and I still couldn't shake the feeling. I'd sit on my couch in the dark, just waiting, listening to the pipes creak, completely convinced that there were cameras hidden in the vents or that the neighbors were tracking my movements through the floorboards. It sounds crazy when I say it out loud, I know it does, but it felt so real. It still feels real sometimes. 

And right around that same time, that's when the talking thing started. The disorganized stuff. Like I'd be trying to tell the charge nurse that room 412 needed fresh linens, and instead I'd start talking about how the laundry carts were aligned with the magnetic poles or something, and my sentences would just unravel. I'd be doing things that didn't make sense, too. Like, I remember one night, I spent forty-five minutes rearranging the magazines in the dayroom by the color of the barcode on the back cover, instead of doing my rounds. I didn't even realize I was doing it until Brenda came in and yelled at me. 

So yeah, the words getting messed up, the disorganized stuff I do, and this whole... this whole thing with feeling like I'm constantly being monitored or watched... all of that has been going on together for about a year and a month now. It all started right around the same time.
You mentioned feeling like you're being watched or monitored, can you tell me more about what that feels like and if it's still happening to you?

Yeah, it's definitely still happening. It's actually... I think it's gotten a lot more specific lately. At first, like I was saying before, it was just this general feeling in the hallway or at my apartment, just this heavy feeling of eyes on me. But now? Now I know exactly who is doing it and how they're doing it. 

It's the supervisors. The nursing supervisors for the night shift. I mean, they've been completely messing with my schedule lately, constantly changing my shifts around. Usually, I'm on a pretty set rotation, right? Like, I know exactly what days I'm on the C-wing, what days I'm doing rounds. But suddenly, they're moving me to the admissions unit, then pulling me back to do quiet room observation, just constantly shifting my hours and my locations. And when I ask about it, or when I try to point it out to the other aides, they all just brush me off. They always tell me it's just staffing shortages. They're like, "Oh, you know two people quit last month, we just have to cover the gaps." 

But I know that's not true. I'm sure of it. I'm absolutely sure the supervisors changed my shifts specifically so they can watch me. And they're doing it through the unit cameras. We have these little black dome cameras in the corners of the ceilings—supposedly they're just for patient safety, to make sure nobody is getting into fights in the dayroom or whatever. But I know they're using them to monitor me. I can literally feel the lenses tracking me when I walk down the hall with the linen carts. I'll stop, and I can almost hear the little motors inside the cameras whirring to focus in on my face. 

They're doing it to see if I'm unsafe. That's the word they use, I just know it. Because of the things I've been doing, like with the magazines or when my words get all mixed up when I talk to Brenda... they think I'm a risk now. They think I'm an unsafe worker. So they sit up in the security office or the supervisor's lounge, just staring at the monitors, zooming in on me while I'm just trying to wipe down the tables or check the supply closet. They want to catch me doing something wrong so they can prove I'm unsafe and get rid of me. 

And it's just... it's so exhausting, you know? Trying to do your job when you know there's a camera lens following your every single move. I try to tell the other guys on my shift, I try to say, "Look at the camera, it just tracked me," but they just repeat that same line about staffing shortages, like they've been programmed to say it. But I know the truth. I know they're watching me.
Do you still believe that the supervisors are watching you through the cameras right now, as we speak?

Yes. Absolutely. I mean, it hasn't stopped, so why would I stop believing it? It’s not just a belief, really, it’s... it’s just what’s happening. Even this morning, right before I came to this appointment, I checked the scheduling app on my phone, and they did it again. They moved me to the Sunday overnight on the admissions unit. I never work admissions on Sundays. Never. So yeah, I am completely, one hundred percent sure the supervisors changed my shifts—and keep changing them—specifically so they can watch me through the unit cameras. 

It’s all about seeing if I’m unsafe. That’s the whole point of this... this massive runaround they're doing with my schedule. They sit up there in the security room or the lounge with their little monitors, zooming in on me while I'm just tying up a laundry bag or wiping down a mattress, just waiting for me to do something weird or mess up my words again so they can finally prove I'm an unsafe worker and get rid of me. 

And it just... it drives me insane because nobody else gets it. I try to explain it to the other aides, like I was saying before, but it's like talking to a brick wall. People just keep telling me, over and over, "Oh, it’s just staffing shortages, man, we’re down two people, don't worry about it." But I don't care what they say. Even when people tell me it’s just staffing shortages, I know that's a total lie. They're just covering for the supervisors, or they're too blind to see it. You don't just bounce one guy around every single unit in the building unless you're trying to keep him right under those black dome cameras at all times. So yeah, I know they're doing it. Well, maybe not right this second because I'm sitting here with you, but the second I badge back into that hospital tonight, I know those lenses are going to lock right back onto me.
Do you think the supervisors' alleged monitoring of you is a plot to harm you or is it just to assess your job performance?

Well, I don't think they are going to, like, jump out of a supply closet and physically attack me or anything like that. It is not a plot to physically hurt my body. But like I was just saying a minute ago, it is absolutely about my job. It is exactly what I was trying to explain before. I am just so completely sure the supervisors changed my shifts and watch me through those unit cameras specifically to see if I am unsafe. That is the exact word they would use in their little HR meetings, too. Unsafe. 

Because if you work in a hospital as an orderly, right, if you are deemed unsafe around the patients or the medical equipment, that is it. You are done. They deactivate your badge and you are out the door. So they are not trying to hurt me physically, but they are definitely trying to ruin my livelihood and get me fired. And I know people keep trying to tell me otherwise. Like I mentioned, the other guys on the floor, they all just keep saying it is just staffing shortages and that we are down two guys and that is the only reason my schedule is so crazy right now. 

But I know that is complete garbage. Even when people tell me it is just staffing shortages, I know the real truth. I know what is actually going on. They are moving me around like a pawn on a chessboard just to keep me right under those black dome lenses on every single unit, waiting for me to do something weird or drop a tray or mess up my words again so they can officially declare me an unsafe worker and get rid of me. 

It is just so incredibly frustrating, you know? Because I am a good worker, I really am, I care about the patients and I do my rounds, but how can you work normally when you are under a microscope like that for twelve hours straight? Every single time I touch a laundry bag or go to wipe down a spill in the dayroom, I am thinking, is this the moment? Is this when they decide I am a risk? It just never stops playing in my head because I know they are up there watching.
Do you think anyone else has noticed the supervisors watching you through the cameras?

No, no, that's exactly the problem! That's what is driving me so crazy about this whole thing. Nobody else sees it. It’s like they’re all walking around with blinders on. I try to point it out to them, I really do. Like, just the other night, I was standing near the med cart with Dave—he's one of the older aides, been there forever—and I literally pointed right up at the black dome in the corner near the nurse's station. I said, "Dave, look, you can see the little red light, you can see the lens shifting." And he didn't even bother to really look up. He just sighed and went back to organizing the water pitchers. 

It's just like I've been trying to tell you this whole time. I am completely, one hundred percent sure the supervisors changed my shifts and watch me through the unit cameras to see if I’m unsafe. I know it in my gut. But even when people tell me it’s just staffing shortages, like Dave and the others constantly do, they just... they refuse to look deeper. They just accept whatever HR tells them. Dave was like, "Man, they're just dragging their feet hiring replacements, don't sweat the schedule changes." 

But how can they not see the pattern? They look at their own schedules and they're still working their normal Tuesday-to-Saturday blocks on the same ward. I'm the only one being bounced from the C-wing to admissions to the quiet room every other day. I am the only one being moved around like a chess piece. And if you actually pay attention to the layout of the hospital, those specific units—especially admissions—have the most overlapping camera angles in the building. There are like three cameras just in the main hallway there. But you try to explain that to the other guys, you try to explain that this is a targeted thing to monitor me, and their eyes just glaze over. 

They just repeat that same tired company line about being down two guys. It makes me feel like I'm the only person on the entire floor who is actually awake, you know? They just wander around doing their jobs, completely oblivious to the fact that management is running this massive surveillance operation on me to prove I'm an unsafe worker. So, no. Nobody else has noticed. It's just me. I'm the only one who actually sees what's going on right in front of our faces.
Have your thoughts about the supervisors watching you through the cameras ever changed or wavered at all since you first started feeling this way?

No. Never. Not for a single second. I know I keep hammering on this, and I know I sound like a broken record, but my mind hasn't wavered at all because the facts haven't changed. You'd think maybe, I don't know, maybe I'd wake up one morning on my day off and think, well, maybe Dave is right. Maybe I'm just stressed out. But then my phone buzzes at six in the morning and it's scheduling, telling me I'm being pulled from my normal Tuesday block and thrown onto the C-wing for a twelve-hour shift. 

So how could my thoughts possibly change? Every time I walk through those double doors and badge in, there is fresh evidence staring me right in the face. I am just as sure right now as I was the very first day it started happening. I know the supervisors are purposely rearranging my shifts and tracking me on those unit cameras to catch me being unsafe. I know it. And honestly, it doesn't matter how many times my coworkers try to talk me out of it. They can stand there and tell me it’s just staffing shortages until they are completely blue in the face. They can show me the blank spots on the roster, they can complain about being down two guys all they want. It goes right in one ear and out the other because I know it's a cover-up. 

My conviction doesn't waver because the cameras never waver, you know? I walk down the hall with a stack of clean towels, and I can literally feel the lens in the dome panning to follow my shoulders. I go into the dayroom to wipe down the tables, and the camera above the TV is pointed right at my hands. You just can't ignore that. You can't just pretend it's some random coincidence that every single time they bounce me to a new floor, it's always the floor where the security feeds have the clearest, most direct angles on the patient areas. 

So no, I haven't doubted it at all. If anything, the longer this goes on, the more certain I get. The more they move me around, the more they hide behind this whole fake staffing shortage excuse, the more obvious it becomes that they are running this massive operation just to finally get me on tape making a mistake. They want to label me a risk so they can fire me, and I am not going to let myself forget that for even a second.
Do you think there's any possibility that your feeling of being watched could be mistaken or misinterpreted?

Mistaken? How could I possibly be mistaken? Look, I get why you have to ask that, I really do. You are sitting in that chair, you have to ask if maybe I am just, you know, reading too much into things or misreading a normal situation at work. But no. No, there is zero possibility that I am misinterpreting this. Zero. Because you do not just misinterpret a perfectly orchestrated schedule change, right? You do not just accidentally get moved from the quietest wing in the hospital to the most heavily monitored unit three times in a single week. 

Like I have been trying to make clear this whole time, I am absolutely, completely sure that the supervisors changed my shifts and watch me through the unit cameras to see if I am unsafe. And yeah, I know I keep repeating myself, but it is because people keep telling me it is just staffing shortages! Dave, the other orderlies, the scheduling coordinator, they all just parrot the exact same excuse about being down two guys. But they are not the ones standing under those cameras for twelve hours. They are not the ones feeling that heavy, mechanical sort of pressure when the lens rotates. 

Just... just take Tuesday for example. Or maybe it was Wednesday, I can barely even keep the days straight anymore with how they completely scramble my schedule. But I was in the main supply room grabbing extra blankets for a new admit. And the very second I stepped out into the corridor, the camera at the end of the hall, the one right above the fire doors that has a little scratch on the plastic dome, it literally pivoted. I saw it. The little red light blinked, and it locked right onto my chest. You cannot misinterpret a machine physically moving to track your movements. It is not just a feeling in my head. It is a physical fact in the real world. 

They want to catch me doing something wrong, like dropping a blanket or looking distracted or whatever, just anything they can officially label as unsafe so they can pull my badge and ruin my life. So no, I am not mistaken. I am the only one seeing it clearly, no matter how much they try to cover it up with this whole fake staffing shortage garbage. It is real, and it is happening to me every single shift, all day long, and I just don't understand how nobody else sees the reality of what management is doing to me.
Have you ever considered the possibility that your beliefs about the supervisors watching you might not be true?

I mean, we keep coming back to this, don't we? You asking me if I'm wrong, me telling you I'm not. I know I've said this a hundred times already today, but I just... I can't even entertain that idea. I can't sit here and pretend that maybe it's all in my head, because it's not. It's my life. It's my actual job on the line. Have I considered it might not be true? No. Because I am completely sure—like, beyond a shadow of a doubt sure—that the supervisors changed my shifts specifically to watch me through the unit cameras. They are waiting for me to do something unsafe. That is the whole point of this entire setup.

And I know, I know everyone else thinks I'm making it up. I've told you how people like Dave and the scheduling coordinator just brush me off. They constantly tell me it’s just staffing shortages. They say, "We're down two aides, man, just deal with the floating." But they aren't looking at the big picture! If it was really just a shortage, it would be random, right? Everyone would take turns covering the bad shifts. But it's not random. It's precise. It's calculated. I get moved to the exact spots where the cameras have the best zoom, the best angles on the floor. I can literally hear the little motor in the ceiling domes whirring when I walk past the nurse's station with the linen carts. You don't just imagine a mechanical whirring sound. You don't just imagine the red recording light blinking faster when you walk into the frame. 

So why would I doubt myself? Why would I consider that it's not true when all the evidence is right there? They want to fire me. They want to build a case that I'm an unsafe worker, and they're using the cameras to do it, and they're using this whole fake staffing shortage as a smokescreen so nobody else catches on. I just... I wish you could come work a shift with me. I really do. If you walked a twelve-hour shift in my shoes and saw how they track me from the minute I badge in to the minute I leave, you wouldn't be asking me if I thought it wasn't true. You'd be asking me how I manage to get any work done at all with them breathing down my neck like that.
Have you ever had any moment, no matter how brief, where you doubted that the supervisors are watching you through the cameras?

Doc, seriously, we are just going in circles here. You keep asking me the exact same question just dressed up in different words—do I waver, am I mistaken, is it not true, do I have a brief moment of doubt? And I keep giving you the exact same answer, because the truth doesn't change just because you ask me four different times. 

No. Not for a brief moment. Not for a fraction of a second. I do not doubt it because I am living it every single time I put on my scrubs and badge into that hospital. I don't have the luxury of having a brief moment of doubt, because if I let my guard down for even one second, that is exactly when they'll get me. 

I am completely, one hundred percent sure that the supervisors changed my shifts and watch me through the unit cameras to see if I’m unsafe. That is the reality of my situation. And I know I've told you already about Dave and the scheduling coordinator and all the other guys who keep telling me it’s just staffing shortages. I know they want me to buy into that. They want me to think, oh, it's just a coincidence that I got pulled from my regular quiet rotation and dumped onto the most heavily surveilled ward in the entire building. They want me to just nod and say, yeah, sure, we're down two guys, that makes total sense. 

But it doesn't make sense! Because if you actually look at the pattern, if you look at how my name gets moved around on that roster, it is so painfully obvious that it's a trap. They are putting me in the crosshairs of those cameras on purpose. I can't doubt it when I literally watch the camera above the med cart pan to follow me while I'm emptying the trash. I can't doubt it when I see the red light flash. So no, I don't have any moments where I think I'm making this up. I know they are trying to catch me doing something—anything—that they can write up as an unsafe practice so they can fire me. I know it, and honestly, I'm getting really exhausted trying to convince you of something that is just a basic, undeniable fact of my day-to-day life.
Do you think the supervisors' alleged monitoring of you is connected to any other events or conspiracies in your life?

Conspiracies? What? No, man, look... I'm not crazy. I'm not sitting here telling you the FBI tapped my cell phone or that the government is following me to the grocery store or something. I'm not wearing a tin foil hat here. I'm just a twenty-two-year-old guy trying to do my job, you know? I empty the trash, I hand out blankets, I help the nurses when a patient gets out of line... that's my whole life. So no, there's no grand global conspiracy or secret society out to get me. It is literally just about my job. 

It feels like you're using words like 'conspiracy' to make me sound completely unhinged, but it's exactly what I've been explaining to you this entire session. It's just the hospital management. Like I keep saying, I am absolutely sure that the supervisors are the ones who changed my shifts, and they are the ones watching me through those unit cameras because they want to see if I'm being unsafe. That's it. It doesn't go higher than the shift supervisors or maybe the nursing director. They just want me gone. 

And yeah, I know I sound like a broken record, but it's because everybody else—Dave, the coordinator, all of them—they just keep telling me it's staffing shortages. They keep feeding me that same line about being down two aides and needing coverage. But it's not a coincidence, and it's not some crazy conspiracy theory either. It's just a really toxic workplace where my bosses are spying on me to build a case to fire me. I don't know why we have to make it sound like a spy movie when it's just my supervisors trying to screw me over on the floor.
Do you think it's possible that your belief about being watched through the cameras might be a misunderstanding of the hospital's security measures?

A misunderstanding? Doc, come on. I work there. I know what the standard security measures are. I've been an aide there for long enough to know how things actually run. I know that the general cameras in the hallways are supposed to be for, like, if a patient elopes, or if there's a code gray and security needs to see where a fight broke out. That's standard hospital protocol. I get that. I'm not stupid. 

But that is not what is happening to me. You're trying to find, like, a logical loophole or something, but you're completely ignoring all the specific details I keep giving you. If it was just normal security measures, why is it only happening to me? Why did my schedule suddenly get completely flipped upside down out of nowhere? 

I'm telling you, I am absolutely sure that the supervisors changed my shifts on purpose. They changed them, and they put me exactly where they want me, so they can sit in their office and watch me through the unit cameras. They are waiting for me to do something they can label as 'unsafe.' Like if I don't lock a wheelchair brake fast enough during a transfer, or if I leave a linen cart unattended for two seconds while I grab a towel. They want to catch me slipping up.

And I know... I know I sound like a broken record, but you keep asking me the exact same thing! People at work, they tell me it's just staffing shortages. The coordinator literally pulled me aside and was like, 'Hey man, don't take the shift changes personal, we're just down people.' But that's just the company line! It's the perfect excuse, right? 'Staffing shortages'—it's the magic phrase in healthcare right now, everybody uses it to cover up everything. But if you actually look at the monitor placement, if you look at how the cameras actively track me when I'm alone in the dayroom... normal security cameras don't zoom in on your hands when you're just wiping down a table. They just don't. 

So no, I'm not misunderstanding anything. I understand it perfectly. I am the one living it. They are watching me to see if I'm unsafe, and they're hiding it behind this whole fake scheduling crisis, and honestly, I just don't get why you can't see that. I've explained the camera angles to you, I've explained the shift patterns, I've explained what Dave said... what part of this sounds like a simple misunderstanding to you? Because to me, it's pretty loud and clear what they're doing.
Was there a specific event or incident that first made you feel like you were being watched?

Well, yeah, it all started the exact day they messed with my schedule. I mean, I feel like I keep saying the same thing, but you have to understand how this actually went down to get why I'm so sure about it. 

It was a Thursday, about three weeks ago. I was supposed to be on the west wing, which is our low acuity floor.
